root.note: The trail stops here. The oldest form we have is Spanish itself, around 1200. Everything earlier is a theory.

history: One of the first words you learn in Spanish is also one of the most mysterious. Nobody knows where perro comes from. It appears around 1200 as a rude word for a mongrel, and soon starts pushing out the normal word can, from Latin canis. Corominas thought it imitated a growl: perr, perr, a sound shepherds used to urge on their dogs. Galician apurrar, ‘to set dogs on’, is offered in support. Others prefer a language older than Latin, which might also connect it to zorro, ‘fox’. The 1737 Academy dictionary tried Greek pyr, ‘fire’, for the dog's fiery temperament, which is not taken seriously now. The honest answer: unknown.
historyEinfach: Perro means ‘dog’, but nobody knows where the word comes from. We first see it about 800 years ago, as a rude word for a bad dog. Slowly it took the place of the old word can, from Latin. Maybe it copies a sound that shepherds made to their dogs. Maybe it is older than Latin. We don't know.

elsewhere.text: Spanish's neighbours all use other words: Catalan gos, Basque txakur, French chien, Galician-Portuguese can. None of them helps to explain perro.
French has no perro. That is part of the mystery: the word has no clear relatives next door.
